questions.stem: In the Uranus myth, which children did Uranus imprison in Tartarus?
questions.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies that Uranus imprisoned only the Hecatoncheires and Cyclopes, not the Titans.
questions.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
questions.alignmentNote: Directly from the myth narrative knowledge node (B1.1 is for text types; B1.2 is for understanding adapted texts).
questions.stemIntent: Check whether student knows which specific children were imprisoned, addressing the common error that all were imprisoned.
questions.commonMisconception: Student thinks Uranus imprisoned all his children (including Titans).

options.label: A
options.text: All his children, including the Titans
options.feedbackWrong: Uranus did not imprison the Titans. He only imprisoned the Hecatoncheires and Cyclopes.

options.label: B
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Uranus was afraid of the Hecatoncheires and Cyclopes, so he locked them in Tartarus.

options.label: C
options.feedbackWrong: The Titans were not imprisoned. In fact, they later rebelled against Uranus.

options.label: D
options.feedbackWrong: He also imprisoned the Cyclopes. Both groups were sent to Tartarus.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the word 'banish'?
questions.successCriteria: Student correctly selects that banish means to permanently expel someone from a place.
questions.ossdExpectation: Use a variety of strategies to build vocabulary.
questions.alignmentNote: Targets vocabulary building – SE B3.1 is for using strategies to build vocabulary.
questions.stemIntent: Check understanding of the word 'banish', which was explicitly taught with the definition 'expel permanently'.
questions.commonMisconception: Student confuses 'banish' with 'imprison' (lock up) or 'kill' (cause death).

options.label: A
options.text: To lock someone in a prison
options.feedbackWrong: That is 'imprison'. Banish means to force someone to leave a place permanently.

options.label: B
options.text: To force someone to leave a place permanently
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Banish means to officially send someone away as a punishment.

options.label: C
options.text: To kill someone for a crime
options.feedbackWrong: That is 'execute' or 'put to death'. Banish does not mean kill.

options.label: D
options.feedbackWrong: That is not the definition. Banish is an official action, not just scaring.

questions.stem: According to the myth, who was the very first being to exist?
questions.successCriteria: Student identifies that Chaos was the first being, not Gaia.
questions.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
questions.alignmentNote: Tests understanding of character roles and origin sequence from the myth.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student knows that Chaos preceded Gaia, not the other way around.
questions.commonMisconception: Student thinks Gaia was the first being because she is Mother Earth and created Uranus.

options.label: A
options.feedbackWrong: Gaia was not first. Chaos existed before Gaia emerged.

options.label: B
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! The myth begins with Chaos, then Gaia, Tartarus, and Eros appeared.

options.label: C
options.feedbackWrong: Uranus was created by Gaia later. The first being was Chaos.

options.label: D
options.feedbackWrong: Chronos is a Titan born later. The very first being was Chaos.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a theme supported by the Uranus myth?
questions.successCriteria: Student selects a theme that is explicitly present in the myth (fear leading to harmful choices, power must be fair, responsibility to oppose injustice, or family conflicts escalate).
questions.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
questions.alignmentNote: SE B1.5 specifically mentions identifying literary elements and themes.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student can select a theme that fits the myth narrative, avoiding themes like love or betrayal that are not central.
questions.commonMisconception: Student chooses a theme not supported by the myth (e.g., love triumphs over all).

options.label: A
options.feedbackWrong: Love is not a main theme in this myth. The story focuses on power, fear, and rebellion.

options.label: B
options.text: Fear can lead people to make harmful choices
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Uranus feared his children and imprisoned them, which led to his downfall.

options.label: C
options.feedbackWrong: Although betrayal occurs (Chronos betrays Uranus), the myth does not clearly show it being punished. Instead, Chronos becomes ruler.

options.label: D
options.feedbackWrong: This theme is not present. The myth is about power struggles and consequences of fear.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects an answer indicating that Uranus imprisoned all his children, including the Titans.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student thinks Uranus imprisoned all his children, but he only imprisoned the Hecatoncheires and Cyclopes. The Titans were left free and later rebelled.

miniLesson.explain: In the myth, Uranus was afraid of his children's power. He imprisoned only the Hecatoncheires (100-armed giants) and the Cyclopes (one-eyed builders) in Tartarus. The Titans, including Chronos, were not imprisoned. They remained free and later, led by Chronos, rebelled against Uranus.
miniLesson.example: Uranus imprisoned the Hecatoncheires and Cyclopes in Tartarus because he feared they would overthrow him. The Titans were not imprisoned. In fact, Chronos, a Titan, used a sickle made by Gaia to defeat Uranus.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Uranus only locked up the 'monsters' (Hecatoncheires and Cyclopes), not the 'gods' (Titans).

guidedPractice.prompt: Who did Uranus imprison? Choose the correct group: A) All his children, B) Only the Hecatoncheires and Cyclopes, C) Only the Titans, D) Only the Cyclopes.
guidedPractice.answer: B) Only the Hecatoncheires and Cyclopes

guidedPractice.prompt: Explain why Uranus did not imprison the Titans.
guidedPractice.answer: Uranus did not imprison the Titans because he only feared the power of the Hecatoncheires and Cyclopes. The Titans were his other children and were not seen as immediate threats. Later, the Titans, led by Chronos, rebelled against Uranus.

guidedPractice.prompt: Why is it important to know that Uranus did not imprison all his children? How does this affect the story's outcome?
guidedPractice.answer: It is important because it shows that Uranus's fear was selective. If he had imprisoned all his children, the Titans would not have been free to rebel. Their rebellion led to Uranus's defeat and the establishment of a new order under Chronos. This detail supports the theme that people have a responsibility to oppose injustice.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects a definition that confuses banish with imprison or kill.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student thinks 'banish' means to imprison or kill, but it means to permanently expel someone from a place.

miniLesson.explain: The word 'banish' means to force someone to leave a place permanently, often as a punishment. It is different from 'imprison' (lock up) or 'kill' (cause death). In the Uranus myth, Uranus imprisoned his children in Tartarus; he did not banish them. Banishment would have meant sending them away forever, not locking them in a prison.
miniLesson.example: If the king banishes a criminal, the criminal must leave the kingdom and cannot return. In contrast, if the king imprisons the criminal, the criminal is kept in a jail.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of 'banish' as 'ban' + 'ish' — you put a ban on someone, forcing them to leave permanently.

guidedPractice.answer: To permanently expel someone from a place.

guidedPractice.prompt: Use the word 'banish' in a sentence about the Uranus myth. (Hint: Think about what Uranus did to his children and how banish is different.)
guidedPractice.answer: Uranus imprisoned his children, but if he had banished them, they would have been sent away permanently.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read the following sentence: 'Chronos banished Uranus after defeating him.' Based on the myth, is this statement true or false? Explain your answer using the definition of banish.
guidedPractice.answer: False. The myth does not say that Chronos banished Uranus. It says Chronos defeated Uranus and became ruler. Banish means to permanently expel, so if Chronos banished Uranus, he would have sent him away forever. The myth does not mention that.

reteachModules.trigger: Selects Gaia as the first being or says she created everything.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes Gaia was the first being or that she created everything, but the myth begins with Chaos. Gaia emerged from Chaos and later created Uranus, but she did not create Chaos, Tartarus, or Eros.

miniLesson.explain: In the Greek myth, the first being was not Gaia but Chaos. From Chaos came Gaia (Earth), Tartarus (the underworld), and Eros (love). Later, Gaia created Uranus (the sky), but she did not create everything. She was not the origin of the universe.
miniLesson.example: The myth says: 'First there was Chaos. Then Gaia, the Earth, appeared.' So Gaia is not the very first being. She created Uranus, but Chaos, Tartarus, and Eros already existed before her creations.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Chaos first, then Gaia. Gaia is a creator, but not the first.

guidedPractice.prompt: Who was the very first being in the Greek myth? A) Gaia B) Chaos C) Uranus
Explain why Gaia is not the first being in the myth.
guidedPractice.answer: The myth begins with Chaos. Gaia emerged from Chaos, so she is not the first being. She came after Chaos.

guidedPractice.prompt: A classmate says, 'Gaia created the whole world, so she is the most powerful being from the start.' How would you correct them using details from the myth?
guidedPractice.answer: I would say that Gaia did not create everything. According to the myth, Chaos existed first, then Gaia appeared. She then created Uranus, but Chaos, Tartarus, and Eros already existed. So Gaia was not the first being, and she did not create the entire world from nothing.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects a theme not supported by the Uranus myth (e.g., love, betrayal, hard work).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student may think any general positive or negative statement can be a theme, without checking if it is directly supported by the events of the myth.

miniLesson.explain: A theme is a core lesson or message that the story teaches. In the Uranus myth, the main themes are about fear leading to harmful choices, power needing to be fair, responsibility to oppose injustice, and family conflicts escalating. To identify a theme, ask: 'What does this story show about life or human nature?' Then check if the story's events actually support that message.
miniLesson.example: For the Uranus myth, the theme 'Fear can lead people to make harmful choices' is supported because Uranus feared his children and imprisoned them, which led to his downfall. The theme 'Love can overcome any obstacle' is not supported because love is not a major factor in the story.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Theme = Story's lesson. Ask 'What does the story teach?' and check the events.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which theme is supported by the Uranus myth? A) Love conquers all  B) Fear leads to harmful choices  C) Hard work pays off
guidedPractice.answer: B) Fear leads to harmful choices

guidedPractice.prompt: Read this statement: 'The theme of the Uranus myth is that people have a responsibility to stand up against unfair systems.' Is this a valid theme for the myth? Explain why or why not using evidence from the story.
guidedPractice.answer: Yes, it is valid. Chronos stood up against Uranus's unfair imprisonment of his children. This shows a responsibility to oppose injustice.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write a short paragraph (3-4 sentences) explaining one theme from the Uranus myth and how two different events in the story support that theme. Use specific characters and actions.
guidedPractice.answer: One theme is 'Fear leads to harmful choices.' Uranus feared his powerful children, so he imprisoned the Hecatoncheires and Cyclopes in Tartarus. This fear-driven action caused Gaia to plot against him, leading to his overthrow by Chronos. Thus, Uranus's harmful choice backfired due to his fear.

reteachModules.trigger: Student writes a connection without a prescribed sentence starter or uses an incomplete sentence.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student thinks they can write a connection as a short phrase or note, not realizing it must start with a sentence starter and be a complete sentence to clearly express the idea.

miniLesson.explain: When making a personal or world connection to the myth, you must use a sentence starter from the lesson and write a complete sentence. A complete sentence has a subject and a verb and expresses a full thought. The starter helps the reader understand the type of connection. Without a starter or with a fragment, your connection is unclear.
miniLesson.example: Bad: 'Reminds me of when I made a bad choice.' (incomplete, no starter) Good: 'This story reminds me of a time when I made a bad choice because I was afraid.' (starter + complete sentence)

guidedPractice.prompt: Complete the sentence using the starter 'This story reminds me of...': This story reminds me of ________________________________.
guidedPractice.answer: This story reminds me of a time when I felt scared of losing something important.

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite the following connection to include a sentence starter and make it a complete sentence: 'Connects to a leader making unfair choices.' Use 'This story connects to...'
guidedPractice.answer: This story connects to a news story about a leader making unfair decisions.

guidedPractice.prompt: Think about a personal experience where fear led to a bad choice. Write one complete sentence connecting it to the Uranus myth. Start with 'This story reminds me of...'
guidedPractice.answer: This story reminds me of a time when I was afraid of losing a friend and made a decision I regret.

[err-connection-format] Student writes a connection without a complete sentence or sentence starter.: Your connection needs to use a sentence starter and be a complete sentence. Let's practice.

cards.question: In the Uranus myth, which children did Uranus imprison in Tartarus?
options: All his children, including the Titans
cards.diagnosis: Check whether student knows which specific children were imprisoned, addressing the common error that all were imprisoned.
misconceptions: Uranus did not imprison the Titans. He only imprisoned the Hecatoncheires and Cyclopes.
✓ Correct! Uranus was afraid of the Hecatoncheires and Cyclopes, so he locked them in Tartarus.
The Titans were not imprisoned. In fact, they later rebelled against Uranus.
He also imprisoned the Cyclopes. Both groups were sent to Tartarus.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies that Uranus imprisoned only the Hecatoncheires and Cyclopes, not the Titans.
cards.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
cards.alignmentNote: Directly from the myth narrative knowledge node (B1.1 is for text types; B1.2 is for understanding adapted texts).
cards.commonMisconception: Student thinks Uranus imprisoned all his children (including Titans).

cards.question: Which of the following best defines the word 'banish'?
options: To lock someone in a prison
To force someone to leave a place permanently
To kill someone for a crime
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding of the word 'banish', which was explicitly taught with the definition 'expel permanently'.
misconceptions: That is 'imprison'. Banish means to force someone to leave a place permanently.
✓ Correct! Banish means to officially send someone away as a punishment.
That is 'execute' or 'put to death'. Banish does not mean kill.
That is not the definition. Banish is an official action, not just scaring.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly selects that banish means to permanently expel someone from a place.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use a variety of strategies to build vocabulary.
cards.alignmentNote: Targets vocabulary building – SE B3.1 is for using strategies to build vocabulary.
cards.commonMisconception: Student confuses 'banish' with 'imprison' (lock up) or 'kill' (cause death).

cards.question: According to the myth, who was the very first being to exist?
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows that Chaos preceded Gaia, not the other way around.
misconceptions: Gaia was not first. Chaos existed before Gaia emerged.
✓ Correct! The myth begins with Chaos, then Gaia, Tartarus, and Eros appeared.
Uranus was created by Gaia later. The first being was Chaos.
Chronos is a Titan born later. The very first being was Chaos.
cards.successCriteria: Student identifies that Chaos was the first being, not Gaia.
cards.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
cards.alignmentNote: Tests understanding of character roles and origin sequence from the myth.
cards.commonMisconception: Student thinks Gaia was the first being because she is Mother Earth and created Uranus.

cards.question: Which of the following is a theme supported by the Uranus myth?
options: Fear can lead people to make harmful choices
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can select a theme that fits the myth narrative, avoiding themes like love or betrayal that are not central.
misconceptions: Love is not a main theme in this myth. The story focuses on power, fear, and rebellion.
✓ Correct! Uranus feared his children and imprisoned them, which led to his downfall.
Although betrayal occurs (Chronos betrays Uranus), the myth does not clearly show it being punished. Instead, Chronos becomes ruler.
This theme is not present. The myth is about power struggles and consequences of fear.
cards.successCriteria: Student selects a theme that is explicitly present in the myth (fear leading to harmful choices, power must be fair, responsibility to oppose injustice, or family conflicts escalate).
cards.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
cards.alignmentNote: SE B1.5 specifically mentions identifying literary elements and themes.
cards.commonMisconception: Student chooses a theme not supported by the myth (e.g., love triumphs over all).

cards.question: Write one sentence connecting the Uranus myth to a personal experience or a world event. Use a sentence starter from the lesson (e.g., 'This story reminds me of...' or 'This connects to...').
cards.diagnosis: Check if students can use a prescribed sentence starter and write a complete sentence connecting the myth to real life, addressing the common error of writing incomplete or starter-free sentences.
cards.successCriteria: Student writes a complete sentence that starts with an appropriate sentence starter and makes a valid connection to the myth.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the rights and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship, and of the contributions of diverse groups to Canadian society.
cards.alignmentNote: D2.3 is about awareness of diversity, but the lesson's real-world connections align with applying themes to society. Alternative: C1.1 for writing short texts. Using D2.3 as it connects to societal awareness.
cards.commonMisconception: Student writes a fragment or omits the sentence starter, or writes a connection that is unclear or irrelevant.
